newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs in Croatia complete "free and fair" vote.
newsitem.headline: Serbs in Croatia complete "free and fair" vote.

text.p: Former rebel Serbs on Monday completed their first vote for six years in a Croatian election, judged by the United Nations to be fair despite technical hitches that almost ruined it on Sunday.
Voting in the Eastern Slavonia enclave, which reverts to Croatian rule this summer after 18 months under U.N. protection, coincided with countrywide local and parliamentary polls held on Sunday.
The ruling nationalist Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) won a landslide victory in 17 of 21 county assemblies nationwide.
It lost only two, while there were stalemates between the HDZ and the opposition in two counties previously run by the nationalists, according to a final unofficial count announced on Monday.

Serbs in Eastern Slavonia got an extra day to vote on Monday to compensate for organisational bungling that led to misplaced and insufficient ballot forms and shut down balloting there for hours on Sunday.
The U.N. blamed the delay on poor planning by authorities, while Zagreb officials put it down to uncertainty over the number of voters, who were still registering as late as Saturday evening.
Franc Vasallo, U.N. election coordinator in Eastern Slavonia, said there was still no way to estimate how many people had actually voted.
U.N. spokesman Philip Arnold said voter turnout on Monday was "a lot lighter than on Sunday" and first unofficial results would be released on Tuesday.

"On behalf of (U.N. administrator Jacques) Klein, I can say that he is confident the election will be certified as fair and free," Arnold told a news conference in Vukovar, Eastern Slavonia's largest city.

Klein, a U.S. general in charge of the mission, has 30 days to formally certify the voting, in which a single Serb party bloc was pitted against the HDZ, backed by Croatian refugees who are keen to reclaim their property.
Eastern Slavonia is the only remaining enclave seized by ethnic Serbs in a war in 1991 yet to be returned to Zagreb's rule.
In Zagreb, an opposition coalition appeared to have edged ahead of the HDZ in elections for the city assembly, reversing the result reported by the state electoral commission earlier in the day.
The earlier report said the HDZ had beaten the allied Social Democrats (SDP) and Social Liberals (HSLS) by a razor-thin margin.
But state electoral commission chairman Ivan Mrkonjic announced later that the SDP had finished with 24.18 percent and HSLS 12.58 percent for a combined 36.76 percent, while the HDZ tallied 35.67.

The reversal did not necessarily mean the opposition would take over the powerful Zagreb regional government, since the HDZ once again reemerged as the biggest single vote getter and its rivals fell well short of a viable majority.

The HDZ lost to a loose seven-party coalition in Zagreb in 1995 but president Franjo Tudjman, citing "national security" as grounds, vetoed four opposition mayoral nominees and imposed a provisional HDZ city administration.

His manoeuvre brought accusations of authoritarianism and was condemned in the West. Tudjman argued the HDZ had won a "relative majority" while the opposition was an unstable mishmash of parties ranging from far left to far right.

Even if this time the opposition takes power in the capital, they could still be obstructed by the HDZ-dominated county assembly, which holds virtually all financial and political power in the region.
The as yet uncounted votes of sailors, convicts and displaced persons might still tip the balance in HDZ's favour in Zagreb.

The SDP and HSLS takeover in Zagreb could depend on whether they can lure to their cause the Peasant Party (HSS), which polled 8.6 percent but has rejected alliances with Social Democrats because of their communist past.

The HDZ, which relied heavily on Tudjman's 'father-of-the-nation" charisma during the campaign, won 41 seats in the parliament's House of Counties. Opposition parties won 22, while two seats will automatically go to Serb representatives from Eastern Slavonia.
